input:
When a pump draws liquid from a tank, it is essential to ensure that the pressure at the pump inlet remains sufficiently high to prevent cavitation, and this is where the concept of available net positive suction head becomes particularly important. In this example, a pump draws condensate from an open tank. Because the tank is open, the pressure acting on the liquid surface is atmospheric pressure, namely 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the condensate at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa. In addition, the static lift, in other words the vertical distance between the liquid surface and the pump, is 1.3 m, and the friction loss in the suction line amounts to 0.6 m. The available net positive suction head, denoted $NPSH_a$, is calculated using the following well-known relation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

In this equation, $P_{atm}$ represents the atmospheric pressure, $P_v$ represents the vapour pressure, $\rho$ represents the density of the liquid, $g$ represents the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ represents the static lift, and $h_f$ represents the friction loss. By substituting the values given above into this equation and carrying out the calculation, the available net positive suction head is found to be 6.4 m. It is important to note that this value must be compared with the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, which is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with an adequate margin in order to ensure reliable and trouble-free operation of the pump.
target:
A pump draws condensate from an open tank, and the available net positive suction head decides whether the pump can operate at its duty flow without cavitation. The quantity is computed from the pressures and levels on the suction side. The tank is open, so the pressure on the liquid surface is atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa. The static lift, the height from the liquid surface to the pump centreline, is 1.3 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.6 m. Available net positive suction head is defined by

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where $P_{atm}$ denotes the pressure on the liquid surface, $P_v$ the vapour pressure, $\rho$ the liquid density, $g$ the gravitational acceleration, $h_{lift}$ the static lift, and $h_f$ the friction loss in the suction line. The first term converts the excess of surface pressure over vapour pressure into a head of liquid. The lift and the friction loss are subtracted because both are spent before the liquid reaches the impeller eye. Substitution of the stated values into the relation gives an available net positive suction head of 6.4 m. The calculation is made at the stated tank level and temperature. A lower tank level raises the static lift and lowers the available head by the same amount; a higher pumping temperature raises the vapour pressure and lowers the pressure term. Either change eats into the margin, so the comparison is made at the least favourable level and temperature the installation can present. The result is a property of the installation, not of the pump. It is checked against the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, which is read from the vendor curve. The available value must exceed the required value, and it must exceed it with margin, because suction conditions vary in service and the vendor value is a test-stand figure. The available head computed here is the figure that comparison starts from.
